# Financial literacy in Bangalore gig workers

<p class="sx-lede">My voicebot assumed that language was what kept people away from financial services. I wanted to measure what else stood in the way.</p>

An empirical study of 40 security guards in gig-style work on the IISc campus in Bangalore. I designed the quiz, administered it in person, analysed the results and wrote the paper as sole author. It was conducted at the Mphasis Sustainability Research Lab, IISc.

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">The question</p>

## Which factor best explains financial literacy among gig workers?

Gig work pays for the days you turn up and rarely comes with insurance, a pension or a fixed income. That makes everyday financial decisions matter more, and mistakes cost more. The security guards I studied share that pattern: they are paid only for the days they work, with one fixed day off a week and long hours.

Before this study I had built a voicebot that answered banking questions in Indian languages, on the assumption that language was the main barrier. This study tested that assumption with primary data. The paper frames financial literacy through Amartya Sen's Capability Approach: knowing how money works is part of what a person is actually able to do.
:::

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">The instrument</p>

## Five questions, rewritten for the lives of the people answering them

The quiz adapts Lusardi and Mitchell's widely used financial-literacy questions. Instead of stocks and mutual funds, it asks about the products the participants actually use: chit funds, fixed deposits, insurance and savings accounts. I designed it with guidance from researchers at the lab.

<ol class="sx-quiz" aria-label="The five quiz questions, from Table 1 of the paper">
<li><b>Numeracy</b>Ravi borrows ₹10,000 at 3% monthly interest. How much interest does he pay each month?</li>
<li><b>Numeracy</b>₹1,000 in a savings account at 5% a year for 5 years: more than, exactly, or less than ₹1,050?</li>
<li><b>Knowledge</b>₹5,000 in a fixed deposit at 5% while inflation is 6%: will it buy more, the same or less than today?</li>
<li><b>Knowledge</b>Raju puts all his savings in one chit fund; Ranganna spreads his across a chit fund, a bank account and insurance. Whose savings are less risky?</li>
<li><b>Awareness</b>True or false: tracking daily expenses can help you avoid running out of money before the month ends.</li>
</ol>

A score of 3 or more counted as financially literate. Each skill area was also scored on its own: a participant was proficient in an area only if every question in it was right.
:::

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">The method</p>

## Two days of fieldwork, and a model chosen for a small sample

::: {.sx-two}

::: {}
The fieldwork ran over two weekend days, 16 and 17 August 2025, in groups of 7 to 10. Each session took about 90 minutes and ended with an open discussion about saving, borrowing, where people get financial advice, and their problems with banks and digital payments.

With 40 people and several predictors, ordinary logistic regression broke down. Some groups answered almost entirely right or wrong, so the model either failed to converge or produced absurd odds ratios. I switched to Bayesian logistic regression with weakly informative priors, which keeps estimates stable on small samples and reports the uncertainty openly as credible intervals.
:::

<ol class="sx-flow" aria-label="How the study ran (simplified from Figure 2 of the paper)">
<li><b>Consent</b><span>Information sheet and consent form for each participant</span></li>
<li><b>Demographics</b><span>Age, gender, education and whether a migrant to Karnataka</span></li>
<li><b>The quiz</b><span>Five questions; the survey and quiz took 20–25 minutes</span></li>
<li><b>Group discussion</b><span>Money habits and challenges; recorded with consent</span></li>
<li><b>Coding</b><span>Literate if 3 or more correct; each skill area scored separately</span></li>
<li><b>Analysis</b><span>Bayesian logistic regression for each outcome</span></li>
</ol>

:::
:::

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">Findings</p>

## Migrant status and age stood out. The intervals are wide, and that matters too

In this sample, migrant workers had much lower odds of being financially literate than workers from Karnataka. Participants aged 30 to 39 did worse on numeracy and knowledge than those under 30. Education level and how literate people thought they were did not reliably predict any outcome.

The width of those intervals is part of the result. With 40 people, the direction is clear but the size is not: the data say migrants did worse, not how much worse.
:::

::: {.sx-section}
<p class="sx-label">Limits and what came next</p>

## What this study can and cannot say

It is a small sample (N = 40) from one kind of gig work at one campus, so it does not represent every gig worker in Bangalore. It is also a single snapshot, so it shows associations, not causes: language, prior financial experience or family support could explain part of the gap.

The paper proposes financial-literacy apps in regional languages, with simple instructions and visual guides, and peer or employer-supported programmes. My next paper, [a literature review on AI and gig work](/projects/literature-review/index-en.html), stays with the same workers.

<blockquote class="sx-pull">
<p>Why would migrants score lower?</p>
<p>The paper suggests two reasons: language barriers, and being far from the trusted people most of us learn about money from. This study cannot tell which matters more. That is the question a larger study would need to answer.</p>
</blockquote>
:::
